facts.title: Two chemists, one element
facts.text: Holmium was identified in 1878-1879 through the work of Swiss chemists Marc Delafontaine and Jacques-Louis Soret, who spotted unknown spectral absorption bands, and independently by the Swedish chemist Per Teodor Cleve. Cleve isolated it from the mineral erbia residues and is usually credited as its principal discoverer. The element was one of several teased apart from the famously tangled rare-earth ores of the 19th century.

facts.title: Named after Stockholm
facts.text: The name holmium comes from Holmia, the Latinized name for Stockholm, the home city of Per Teodor Cleve. It joins a remarkable cluster of elements named after the tiny Swedish village of Ytterby and its region, including yttrium, terbium, erbium, and ytterbium. Few places on Earth have lent their name to so many elements.

facts.title: The magnetic champion
facts.text: Holmium has the highest magnetic moment of any naturally occurring element, about 10.6 Bohr magnetons per atom. Because of this, holmium is used to build the strongest artificial magnetic fields, often as a high-flux pole piece concentrating the field at the center of powerful magnets. This property stems from its many unpaired 4f electrons.

facts.title: A laser for surgery
facts.text: The holmium-doped YAG (Ho:YAG) laser emits infrared light at about 2,100 nanometers, a wavelength strongly absorbed by water in human tissue. Surgeons use it to break up kidney stones and to treat enlarged prostates with minimal bleeding, since the energy is absorbed within a fraction of a millimeter. This precision makes holmium a quiet but important player in modern medicine.

facts.title: Spectral standard ruler
facts.text: Holmium oxide dissolved in perchloric acid produces a set of very sharp, well-defined absorption peaks across the ultraviolet and visible range. These peaks are so stable and reproducible that the solution is used as a wavelength-calibration standard for spectrophotometers worldwide. In effect, holmium serves as a chemical ruler that keeps optical instruments honest.

facts.title: Color that changes with the light
facts.text: Holmium compounds can appear yellow or pinkish-orange, but they show a striking effect called metamerism: their apparent color shifts depending on whether they are viewed under daylight or artificial fluorescent or incandescent light. This happens because holmium's narrow absorption bands interact differently with different light spectra. The same crystal can look noticeably different just by changing the bulb above it.

facts.title: Soft, silvery, and reactive
facts.text: Pure holmium is a relatively soft, silvery-white metal that is malleable enough to be cut and shaped. In dry air at room temperature it is fairly stable, but it slowly tarnishes in moist air and burns readily when heated to form yellowish holmium(III) oxide. Like its lanthanide neighbors, it almost always occurs chemically in the +3 oxidation state.

facts.title: Born in dying stars
facts.text: Holmium is forged in the cosmos mainly by the slow neutron-capture process (the s-process) inside aging giant stars and by the rapid r-process in violent events such as neutron-star mergers. Scattered through the galaxy by these stellar deaths, it became part of the cloud that formed our solar system. Every holmium atom on Earth is recycled stardust.

facts.title: Hidden in monazite sand
facts.text: Despite its rare-earth label, holmium is more abundant in Earth's crust than gold or platinum, at roughly 1.4 milligrams per kilogram. It is never found as a free metal but is extracted from minerals such as monazite and gadolinite, often as a minor component alongside other lanthanides. China currently dominates the mining and refining of these ores.

facts.title: No job in the body
facts.text: Holmium has no known biological role in any living organism, and humans take in only trace amounts through food and water. Its salts show low to moderate toxicity, and the metal dust can be irritating, but it poses little everyday hazard. Researchers do harness radioactive holmium-166, however, to deliver targeted radiation that shrinks tumors and treats certain cancers.
